entities.name: Walter of Saint Omer
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Walter of Saint Omer, also known as Walter of Fauquembergues or Walter of Tiberias, was a pivotal Crusader lord and Prince of Galilee in the Latin Kingdom of Jerusalem, whose life spanned a critical period of consolidation and defense against burgeoning Muslim powers. Born to William II of Saint Omer and Melisinde of Picquigny, his lineage connected him to prominent Frankish nobility and established his place within the military aristocracy of the Levant. His death in 1174 marked the end of a career dedicated to securing the northern frontiers of the Crusader states, embodying the challenges and ambitions of the second generation of Frankish settlers.

Walter's ascent to prominence was largely secured through his marriage to Eschiva of Bures, the heiress to the Principality of Galilee, around 1159. This union transferred the significant strategic territory of Galilee, with its capital at Tiberias, into the hands of the Saint Omer family. As prince, Walter was responsible for defending this vital frontier against incursions from Nur al-Din Zangi's forces and later the nascent Ayyubid Sultanate. He participated in numerous military campaigns, including the siege of Harim in 1164 where he was captured and later ransomed, highlighting the perilous nature of Crusader lordship. His role as Constable of the Kingdom of Jerusalem further underscored his military importance and influence within the High Court, particularly during the regency for the young Baldwin IV.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Walter of Saint Omer significantly contributed to the military and political stability of the northern Latin Kingdom of Jerusalem during a crucial period of Muslim resurgence. His tenure as Prince of Galilee and Constable helped fortify the Crusader states against Nur al-Din and Saladin, directly impacting the kingdom's survival for several decades.
